questions.q: What does Jarvis recommend instead of endless growth?
a: Deliberately capping profit to keep the business small
Hiring a large team as quickly as possible
Raising venture capital to scale faster
Expanding into every market you can reach
questions.why: Lesson 1 says a company of one should set profit limits so the business serves the owner instead of consuming them.

questions.q: What did Sean D'Souza do to keep his business manageable?
a: Set a yearly profit limit of $500,000
Hired a manager to run daily operations
Turned down all clients below a certain size
Moved his office into his home
questions.why: The summary describes Psychotactics capping profit at $500,000 a year so it would not need more staff or time.

questions.q: Why does Jarvis say a niche audience is better than a broad one?
a: You can solve one group's problems far better
It costs less to advertise to a wide market
It lets you raise prices without explanation
It protects you from changes in your industry
questions.why: Lesson 2 argues that going narrow lets you give a specific group exactly what it wants, while generic products lose appeal.

questions.q: What happened to Starbucks when it tried to appeal to everyone?
a: It lost its way and closed around 900 stores
It doubled the number of its locations
It was bought by a larger coffee chain
It stopped selling coffee for a year
questions.why: The summary says Starbucks drifted from its neighborhood coffee-shop vision and later had to return to it after closures.

questions.q: Why does Jarvis advise against large upfront investment?
a: Slow, self-funded growth keeps you independent and in control
Investors usually demand too little of the business
Small businesses cannot use modern technology
Early profits are impossible without outside funding
questions.why: Lesson 3 says venture funding makes you answer to investors, while quick small profits protect your independence.
